topics.title: Introduction & Scope of AS 16
explain: AS 16 prescribes the accounting treatment for borrowing costs incurred by an enterprise.
It does not deal with actual or imputed costs of owners' equity, such as equity share capital and retained earnings.
Preference share capital classified as a liability IS covered under AS 16.
Preference share capital classified as equity is NOT covered under AS 16.
topics.example: A company issues preference shares classified legally as a liability; the interest or dividend cost on them falls under AS 16.
remember: AS 16 excludes equity costs but includes preference shares classified as liabilities.
mistakes: Treating all preference share dividends as excluded from AS 16 without checking if they are classified as liabilities.

quiz.q: Which of the following fund sources is covered under AS 16?
o: Preference Share Capital classified as a liability
Preference Share Capital classified as equity
quiz.why: Preference share capital classified as a liability involves borrowing cost attributes covered by AS 16.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of AS 16?
o: To value inventory at net realisable value
To prescribe accounting treatment for borrowing costs
To record foreign branch translation gains
quiz.why: AS 16 specifically prescribes rules for capitalising or expensing borrowing costs.

topics.title: Definitions of Borrowing Costs & Qualifying Asset
explain: Borrowing costs are interest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with borrowing funds.
Borrowing costs include interest, amortisation of discounts/premiums, amortisation of ancillary costs, finance lease charges, and exchange differences (to interest extent).
A qualifying asset is a tangible or intangible asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale.
A substantial period of time is ordinarily presumed to be 12 months unless a shorter or longer period is justified by facts.
Assets ready for intended use or sale when acquired are not qualifying assets.
topics.example: Constructing a manufacturing plant taking 15 months is a qualifying asset, but buying a ready-to-drive truck is not.
remember: 12 months is the default rebuttable presumption for a substantial period of time.
mistakes: Classifying assets ready for immediate use upon acquisition as qualifying assets.

quiz.q: What is the standard rebuttable presumption period for a 'substantial period of time' under AS 16?
quiz.why: AS 16 ordinarily presumes 12 months as a substantial period of time unless facts justify otherwise.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a qualifying asset under AS 16?
o: Manufacturing plant taking 18 months to construct
Power generation plant taking 2 years to build
Vehicle purchased ready for immediate use
Investment property taking 15 months to construct
quiz.why: Assets ready for intended use when acquired do not require a substantial period to get ready.

topics.title: Exchange Differences on Foreign Currency Borrowings
explain: Exchange differences on principal of foreign currency borrowings are borrowing costs under AS 16 only to the extent of the interest rate differential.
Amount treated under AS 16 is the lower of actual exchange loss OR difference between local currency interest and foreign currency interest.
Any remaining excess exchange loss beyond this differential is accounted for under AS 11.
Subsequent exchange gains in future years reduce borrowing costs to the extent exchange loss was previously capitalised under AS 16.

flow.title: Treatment of Foreign Exchange Loss
steps: Calculate local interest minus foreign interest
Take lower of the two amounts

topics.example: If foreign interest is Rs 24,000, hypothetical local interest is Rs 49,500 (diff = 25,500), and exchange loss is Rs 30,000, then Rs 25,500 goes to AS 16 and Rs 4,500 to AS 11.
remember: AS 16 exchange loss limit = Interest on local currency borrowing minus Interest on foreign currency borrowing.
mistakes: Capitalising the entire foreign exchange loss without capping it at the local interest rate differential.

quiz.q: Foreign interest is Rs 24,000, local interest would be Rs 49,500, and principal exchange loss is Rs 30,000. How much exchange loss is treated under AS 16?
quiz.why: It is capped at the local interest differential of Rs 49,500 - Rs 24,000 = Rs 25,500.

quiz.q: Under which standard is any excess foreign exchange loss beyond the interest differential accounted for?
quiz.why: Excess exchange loss not qualifying as borrowing cost under AS 16 is governed by AS 11.

topics.title: Borrowing Costs Eligible for Capitalisation & Recognition Criteria
explain: Borrowing costs directly attributable to acquisition, construction, or production of a qualifying asset are capitalised.
Directly attributable costs are those that would have been avoided if expenditure on the qualifying asset had not been made.
Capitalisation requires two recognition criteria: future economic benefits are probable, and costs can be measured reliably.
Borrowing costs not directly attributable to qualifying assets are recognized as an expense in P&L.

flow.title: Capitalisation Eligibility Decision
steps: Capitalise cost as part of asset

topics.example: Interest on a loan specifically taken to construct a factory shed is capitalised, whereas interest on a routine working capital loan is expensed in P&L.
remember: Borrowing costs must be avoidable if expenditure on qualifying asset wasn't made to be directly attributable.
mistakes: Capitalising borrowing costs on assets that do not meet the qualifying asset criteria.

quiz.q: How are borrowing costs treated if they are not directly attributable to a qualifying asset?
o: Recognised as an expense in P&L
quiz.why: Borrowing costs not directly linked to qualifying assets must be expensed in the period incurred.

quiz.q: Which condition is required to capitalise borrowing costs?
o: Probable future economic benefits and reliable cost measurement
quiz.why: AS 16 requires probable economic benefits and reliable cost measurement for capitalisation.

topics.title: Specific Borrowings
explain: Specific borrowings are funds obtained specifically for acquiring a particular qualifying asset.
Borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation = Actual borrowing costs incurred minus income earned on temporary investment of those borrowings.
Funds temporarily invested before being spent on the asset reduce the net borrowing cost to be capitalised.

flow.title: Calculating Specific Borrowing Capitalisation Amount
steps: Identify temporary income on unused funds
Deduct temporary income from actual costs

topics.example: If interest on a specific loan is Rs 18 lakhs and Rs 3.5 lakhs is earned by placing idle loan funds in short deposits, net capitalisable cost is Rs 14.5 lakhs.
remember: Net Capitalisable Cost = Actual Interest Incurred - Temporary Investment Income.
mistakes: Crediting temporary investment income to P&L instead of deducting it from capitalised borrowing cost.

quiz.q: How is temporary investment income earned on specific borrowings treated under AS 16?
o: Deducted from borrowing costs to be capitalised
quiz.why: AS 16 mandates deducting income on temporary investments of specific borrowings from interest incurred.

quiz.q: A specific loan incurs interest of Rs 10 lakhs and earns Rs 2 lakhs temporary interest income. What amount is capitalised?
quiz.why: Capitalised amount = Actual interest (10 lakhs) - Temporary income (2 lakhs) = Rs 8 lakhs.

topics.title: General Borrowings & Capitalisation Rate
explain: General borrowings are non-specific pool of funds used partly for qualifying assets.
Capitalisation rate = (Borrowing cost on general borrowings / Weighted average general borrowings outstanding) * 100.
Amount eligible for capitalisation = Expenditure incurred on qualifying asset x Capitalisation rate.
Upper Limit Check: Total capitalised borrowing cost cannot exceed total borrowing costs incurred during that period.
topics.example: If general loans total Rs 14 lakhs with interest of Rs 1,72,000, the capitalisation rate is 12.285%, applied to qualifying expenditures.
remember: Exclude specific borrowings when calculating the general borrowing weighted average rate.
mistakes: Capitalising an amount that exceeds the actual total interest incurred during the period.

quiz.q: Formula for Capitalisation Rate on general borrowings is:
o: (Borrowing cost on general borrowings / Weighted average general borrowings) x 100
quiz.why: AS 16 defines capitalisation rate as borrowing cost on general borrowings divided by weighted average general borrowings.

quiz.q: What is the maximum limit of borrowing costs capitalised on general borrowings?
o: Total borrowing costs incurred during that period
quiz.why: AS 16 caps capitalised borrowing costs at total borrowing costs actually incurred in that period.

topics.title: Carrying Amount Exceeding Recoverable Amount
explain: When carrying amount or expected ultimate cost of a qualifying asset exceeds recoverable amount or NRV, write-down is required.
Write-down or write-off is executed in accordance with applicable Accounting Standards (e.g., AS 28 or AS 2).
Reversals of write-downs are also governed by those specific accounting standards.

flow.title: Asset Impairment Test for Qualifying Assets
steps: Is carrying cost exceeding recoverable amount?
Write down excess cost to recoverable

topics.example: A building under construction has a cost including interest of Rs 60 lakhs, but its recoverable amount is Rs 52 lakhs; Rs 8 lakhs must be written down.
remember: Capitalising interest cannot push an asset's book value above its recoverable amount.
mistakes: Continuing capitalisation without writing down when total accumulated costs exceed recoverable value.

quiz.q: If carrying amount of a qualifying asset exceeds its recoverable amount, what action must be taken?
o: Write down carrying amount to recoverable amount
quiz.why: Excess carrying amount over recoverable amount must be written down as per accounting standards.

quiz.q: Which accounting standards govern the write-down of qualifying assets when cost exceeds recoverable amount?
o: Other applicable standards like AS 28 or AS 2
quiz.why: AS 16 states write-down or write-off follows requirements of other relevant standards.

topics.title: Commencement, Suspension, & Cessation of Capitalisation
explain: Commencement starts when ALL 3 conditions are met: expenditure incurred, borrowing costs incurred, and active preparation activities in progress.
Technical and administrative work prior to physical construction count as active development.
Suspension occurs during extended periods of interrupted active development.
Do NOT suspend capitalisation during temporary delays that are a necessary part of getting asset ready (e.g., high water levels in bridge construction).
Cessation occurs when substantially all activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for intended use/sale are complete.
If construction completes in parts capable of independent use, capitalisation ceases for each part as it completes.

flow.title: Capitalisation Lifecycle
steps: Commence when spend interest work start
Cease when substantially all work completes

topics.example: If a building structure is complete but minor decoration is pending, capitalisation ceases because substantially all activities are complete.
remember: Necessary temporary delays (like seasonal floods during bridge construction) do NOT suspend capitalisation.
mistakes: Continuing capitalisation during decorative or routine cosmetic work after physical construction is complete.

quiz.q: Capitalisation of borrowing costs commences when which of the following conditions is satisfied?
o: Expenditure, borrowing cost, and active preparation activities are all in progress
quiz.why: All three conditions (expenditure, borrowing costs, and active activities) must be simultaneously met.

quiz.q: Construction of a bridge is delayed by 1 month due to seasonal high water levels common to the area. Capitalisation should be:
quiz.why: Temporary delays that are a necessary/normal part of the process do not suspend capitalisation.

topics.title: Disclosure Requirements
explain: Financial statements must disclose the accounting policy adopted for borrowing costs.
Financial statements must disclose the total amount of borrowing costs capitalised during the period.

flow.title: AS 16 Disclosure Checklist
steps: Identify accounting policy for borrowing costs
Calculate total interest capitalised in period
Disclose policy in notes to accounts
Disclose capitalised amount in financial statements

topics.example: A company notes to accounts state: 'Borrowing costs directly attributable to qualifying assets are capitalised. Total interest capitalised during 20X1-20X2: Rs 74,189.'
remember: Both accounting policy AND exact capitalised amount must be disclosed.
mistakes: Disclosing the capitalised amount while omitting the accounting policy adopted.

quiz.q: Which of the following disclosures is explicitly required by AS 16?
o: List of bank branches where loans were taken
Accounting policy adopted for borrowing costs and amount capitalised
Names of board members who approved the loan
quiz.why: AS 16 specifies disclosure of accounting policy and capitalised borrowing cost amount.

quiz.q: How many main disclosure requirements are specified under AS 16?
quiz.why: AS 16 specifies two requirements: policy adopted and amount capitalised.
